lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Compare a small desk sculpture and a public outdoor sculpture with two differences that matter for design.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Outdoor needs weatherproof materials and safer edges; desk piece can be fragile and detailed.'

WATCH FOR
Assuming every sculpture is only for museums. Design purposes vary.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
From an approved source, study one sculptor or designer’s work. Write materials, purpose, site and one process clue you observe. Credit the source.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL

TRY FIRST

teach_steps.explain:
Sculptors and designers solve 3D problems for different purposes: gallery sculpture, playground forms, product design or public statues. Study published examples to notice materials, scale, audience and site. Describe process evidence (maquettes, joins, finishes) rather than inventing private biographies.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the elements, techniques or performance choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For movement or instruments, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby and stop if anything feels unsafe. You may always describe a choice instead of performing it. One deliberate artistic choice with a named effect is more useful than a longer praise sentence.
teach_steps.notice: Assuming every sculpture is only for museums. Design purposes vary. Name the element or technique and its effect, not just decoration.
